support.quote: These species visit in spring to take advantage of the high numbers of insects, but wouldn’t have enough food if they stayed here through winter.

support.quote: The primary motivation for migration appears to be food; for example, some hummingbirds choose not to migrate if fed through the winter.

We have measured heart rates as an estimate of energy expenditure in imprinted great white pelicans (Pelecanus onocrotalus) trained to fly in 'V' formation, and show that these birds save a significant amount of energy by flying in formation.

The well-held belief is that such aggregations give an energetic benefit for those birds that are flying behind and to one side of another bird through using the regions of upwash generated by the wings of the preceding bird
Flying in the V formation is thought by some to improve energy efficiency.
Migratory species in these groups have great difficulty crossing large bodies of water, since thermals only form over land, and these birds cannot maintain active flight for long distances.
it avoids crossing the Mediterranean Sea and detours via the Levant in the east or the Strait of Gibraltar in the west, because the air thermals on which it depends for soaring do not form over water
Our results suggest that young common cuckoos possess an innate migration programme enabling successful migration to wintering grounds independently of adults.
Navigation is often ‘hard-wired’ and shaped by environmental cues like changes in temperature or day length.
Birds rely for navigation on a combination of innate biological senses and experience
Arctic terns hold the record for the longest migration of any animal in the world, annually making the journey from the Arctic Circle to the Antarctic Circle.
The Arctic tern Sterna paradisaea has the longest-distance migration of any bird, and sees more daylight than any other, moving from its Arctic breeding grounds to the Antarctic non-breeding areas.
